explanations.explanation: Mercy, friend. David's first words are “Have mercy on me, O God, according to Your loving devotion…” No excuses and no warm-up speech. He leans on God's loving devotion and great compassion, and he asks.

David doesn't ask for a sign anywhere in this psalm. His very first request is “Have mercy on me, O God…” Nathan, the prophet who came to him, had already spoken, and David turns straight to God. He asks for mercy, and he asks it according to God's loving devotion.

David is a king, so I can see why victory sounds like a good guess. But the psalm never mentions a battle. The first thing he says is “Have mercy on me, O God…” and then he asks God to blot out his transgressions.
It's the other way around, friend. David says, “For I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me.” He isn't confused about it at all. He knows exactly what he did, and he says so to God.
False is right. David says, “For I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me.” There's no fog in that sentence. He knows what he did and he doesn't dodge it.
God. David says, “Against You, You only, have I sinned and done what is evil in Your sight…” He's praying to God, so he says it right to His face. He doesn't hide behind a long explanation either.

Nathan is the prophet who came to David, but David never names him in this psalm. Look at what David says to God: “Against You, You only, have I sinned…” He puts the word only right there. The one he names is God.
David is Israel's king, so Israel is a natural guess. But the psalm never names the nation here. David says, “Against You, You only, have I sinned…” That word only points to one person, and it's God.

True. David says God will be “proved right when You speak and blameless when You judge.” He isn't arguing his case or hunting for a loophole. He says God is in the right, and he's speaking to God Himself.
David says the opposite. He prays that God “may be proved right when You speak and blameless when You judge.” So in this prayer, God is the one in the right. David lays no blame on Him.

David says it goes back much further. He says, “Surely I was brought forth in iniquity; I was sinful when my mother conceived me.” That's the very beginning, not some later chapter of his life. He's being completely honest with God.

False is right. David says, “Surely I was brought forth in iniquity; I was sinful when my mother conceived me.” He doesn't claim a clean record up to some point. He traces it all the way back to the start.
In the inmost being. David says, “Surely You desire truth in the inmost being…” That's the deep inside, the part nobody else sees. And he adds that God teaches him wisdom in the inmost place.

Temple courts sound like a church-answer, and I get why. But David never mentions them here. He says, “Surely You desire truth in the inmost being…” God wants the truth deep inside, not just in a place.
David doesn't mention the city gates in this psalm. He says, “Surely You desire truth in the inmost being…” That's the inside of a person, far from any gate or crowd. It's the deepest spot there is.

David says no such thing. He says, “Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean; wash me, and I will be whiter than snow.” He doesn't mention any leftover stain. When God washes, David says he will be clean.

False is right. David says, “Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean…” He doesn't leave room for a stubborn spot. We've all scrubbed a shirt and still found the mark, but David isn't talking about that kind of wash.

Joy and gladness. David prays, “Let me hear joy and gladness; let the bones You have crushed rejoice.” His bones are crushed and he still asks for joy. I think that's how much he wants God to restore him.
Songs of victory aren't what David asks for. He says, “Let me hear joy and gladness…” It's a quieter request than a victory parade. He wants to hear joy, and he wants his crushed bones to rejoice.

David isn't asking to hear warnings here. He prays, “Let me hear joy and gladness; let the bones You have crushed rejoice.” After the heaviness of the first verses, he asks for something gentle. He wants joy.

Sins. David says, “Hide Your face from my sins and blot out all my iniquities.” Notice it's his own sins he wants hidden, not anybody else's. And he asks again for them to be blotted out, the same word he used at the start.
Enemies don't show up in this verse. David says, “Hide Your face from my sins…” The whole prayer is about his own sin, not anyone chasing him. He keeps the focus where it belongs.
It's an understandable guess with a prayer this heavy. But the verse doesn't mention tears. David says, “Hide Your face from my sins and blot out all my iniquities.” Sins is the word he picks.
A clean heart. David prays, “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.” That's a request for something new on the inside. It goes deeper than washing the outside.
David does talk about singing later in this psalm, so I see the pull. But that's not what he asks God to create. He says, “Create in me a clean heart, O God…”

David never asks for a new name in this psalm. His request is “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.” He's asking for a change on the inside. The name can stay the same.
God's presence. David prays, “Cast me not away from Your presence…” Of everything he could be afraid of losing, he names being near God. I think that tells you what matters most to him right now.

Jerusalem does show up at the end of this psalm, but not here. David says, “Cast me not away from Your presence…” The thing he doesn't want to lose is nearness to God. A place on the map isn't what he's asking about.
David is a king, so the throne is a fair guess. But the verse says, “Cast me not away from Your presence…” He doesn't mention his crown or his throne. He's asking about God.
True. In the same breath David says, “…take not Your Holy Spirit from me.” That's his second request, right alongside not being cast away from God's presence. Two prayers, one right after the other.
David does ask it. He prays, “Cast me not away from Your presence; take not Your Holy Spirit from me.” It's the second half of the same verse. That's two things he asks God not to do.
The joy of His salvation. David asks, “Restore to me the joy of Your salvation…” The word restore tells you he's had that joy before. I bet he's thinking about how much he's missing it.
David doesn't ask about peace or a temple in this verse. He says, “Restore to me the joy of Your salvation…” What he wants back is joy. And it's the joy that comes from God's salvation.

Strength sounds like a kingly request, I'll give you that. But David prays, “Restore to me the joy of Your salvation…” Joy is what he asks God to give back. Then he asks to be sustained with a willing spirit.

Return to God. David says, “Then I will teach transgressors Your ways, and sinners will return to You.” He wants to help other people find their way back. Someone who's been forgiven pointing others to the same God, that's the picture.
David says the opposite. He says, “Then I will teach transgressors Your ways, and sinners will return to You.” Instead of hiding, they come back. He's praying for people to turn toward God.
David doesn't picture anyone arguing here. He says, “Then I will teach transgressors Your ways, and sinners will return to You.” The word is return. They head back to God.
True. David prays, “Deliver me from bloodguilt, O God, the God of my salvation, and my tongue will sing of Your righteousness.” He ties the singing to being delivered. It's a quiet kind of promise.

David does say it. He prays, “Deliver me from bloodguilt, O God, the God of my salvation, and my tongue will sing of Your righteousness.” The singing follows the deliverance. He's promising to sing about God's righteousness.
David says the opposite. He says, “For You do not delight in sacrifice, or I would bring it…” He's saying that if God wanted that, he'd bring it. So it's not what David believes God is after here.

False is right. David says, “For You do not delight in sacrifice, or I would bring it; You take no pleasure in burnt offerings.” He says he would bring one if that's what God wanted. Then he tells us what God does want in the next verse.

A broken spirit. David says, “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit…” After saying God takes no pleasure in burnt offerings, he points to something inside a person. It's an honest, humble spirit before God.

A proud spirit is nearly the opposite of what David says. He says, “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit…” Nothing in this verse about puffing yourself up. He's talking about a spirit that's been humbled.

David doesn't say a fearful spirit. He says, “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise.” The word is broken, and it's paired with a contrite heart.
David says the reverse. He says, “…a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise.” God doesn't turn that heart away. That's a lot of comfort packed into one line.
False is right. David says, “…a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise.” Whoever comes to God with a heart like that, David says, He won't look down on it.

Jerusalem. David prays, “In Your good pleasure, cause Zion to prosper; build up the walls of Jerusalem.” After all that praying about himself, he ends by praying for the city. His prayer opens up wider.
Jericho is a city in the Bible, but it isn't the one in this verse. David prays, “…build up the walls of Jerusalem.” That's the city he names alongside Zion.
Babylon isn't in this psalm at all. David says, “In Your good pleasure, cause Zion to prosper; build up the walls of Jerusalem.” He's praying for the city that goes with Zion.

Righteous. David says, “Then You will delight in righteous sacrifices, in whole burnt offerings…” Notice that word then. After the broken spirit and the prayer for Jerusalem, he says God will delight in them.
David doesn't say grain here. He says, “Then You will delight in righteous sacrifices, in whole burnt offerings…” The word he uses is righteous. It follows right after his prayer for Jerusalem.

Costly is a thoughtful guess, but it isn't David's word. He says, “Then You will delight in righteous sacrifices…” He describes them as righteous, not as expensive. And he names whole burnt offerings and bulls on God's altar.
